implementation_notes: JavaScript has no channel primitive, and the event loop changes the design because nothing blocks a thread. The right primitives are Promise-based: a bounded async queue (an array with a waiting-resolvers list, resolved in FIFO order) is the standard channel, and it must never block - a full queue's send returns a promise that resolves when there is room (backpressure by awaiting), not a blocking put. AbortSignal is the cancellation and the close (aborting wakes every waiter), which is the correct termination model for a non-blocking runtime. async iterators are the pull-based alternative for a stream: an AsyncGenerator is a receive channel that the consumer drives one item at a time, with natural backpressure (the producer suspends at yield until the consumer calls next). For a real MPMC or bounded blocking queue, use a library (p-queue, it-channel) rather than hand-rolling, because the lost-wakeup and fairness details are where hand-rolled versions break. Node's worker_threads MessagePort is a separate message channel between threads.
idiom_name: bounded async queue (array + FIFO resolvers, send returns a promise = backpressure), AbortSignal for close, async generators for pull
pitfalls: Never resolve a send that was waiting and never reject waiters on close: a send/recv promise left pending forever hangs the consumer - AbortSignal must reject every waiter.
A blocking put does not exist in JavaScript: a 'full' channel must return a promise the producer awaits (backpressure), not spin or drop - and awaiting it is what applies backpressure.
A full queue with no backpressure silently drops or grows unboundedly; the cap must be enforced and the drop/wait policy chosen.
An async generator that is not fully consumed (the for-await breaks early) must have .return() called to run its finally, or the underlying resource leaks.
A hand-rolled async queue in a multi-worker setup is where lost wakeups and ordering bugs live; use a library (p-queue, it-channel) for anything beyond a single-threaded producer/consumer.
